generated_by: generated by data/basemap.py; do not edit by hand

projection.name: south polar azimuthal equidistant (same as lib/geometry.ts projectSouthPole)
projection.centre: south pole at the image centre
projection.radius_proportional_to: degrees from the pole (colatitude), so the distance from the centre is linear in latitude
projection.moon_radius_note: 1,737,400 m sphere: the radius of the LOLA DEM datum, data/horizon_mask.py, and lib/geometry.ts (1737.4 km)
projection.orientation: longitude 0 points up the image; east longitude is clockwise (lon 90 is to the right, lon 180 down, lon -90 left)

outside_edge_circle: transparent (alpha 0, grey 0): pixels farther from the centre than size/2

extent.note: ground distance along the surface from the pole to the middle of each side (R * colatitude in radians)

pixel_coordinates: x to the right, y down, pixel edges on whole numbers: the pole is at (size/2, size/2), the top-left pixel covers x 0..1, y 0..1

pixel_to_lat_lon: dx = x - size / 2; dy = size / 2 - y
lon = atan2(dx, dy) in degrees, -180..180, east positive
formulas.as_app_map: this is projectSouthPole(lat, lon, radiusPx = size/2, edgeLatDeg = edge_lat_deg) with the origin moved to (size/2, size/2); scale the pixels by (map radius in SVG units) / (size/2)
formulas.angles_in: degrees for lat/lon and edge_lat_deg (convert to radians for sin and cos)

hillshade.light_azimuth_note: degrees clockwise from the top of the image (315 = upper left)
hillshade.why: the real Sun at the pole is under 2 degrees high, which would make a black picture; a made-up light 20 degrees up and 2x heights make crater walls readable. Not a sunlight map: shadows here say nothing about real illumination.
hillshade.method: standard Lambert hillshade on the heights resampled to the output grid, grey = 255 * (n . light), clipped to 0..1

dem.product: LRO LOLA DEM v4 S Pole, NASA Moon Trek
dem.crs: Moon2000 south polar stereographic, central meridian 0 (heights in metres above the 1,737,400 m sphere)
dem.resampling: averaged down to about one output pixel, then bilinear into the azimuthal equidistant grid

credit: LRO LOLA DEM v4 S Pole (30 m and 5 m), NASA Moon Trek, used for the map hillshade
place_with_pins: draw the image centred on the pole with radius = size/2 map units (or scale it), then draw pins at projectSouthPole(lat, lon, size/2, edge_lat_deg). A tile with a smaller edge_lat_deg (basemap-87.5) covers only the middle of the larger one: its radius in the big tile's pixels is (edge_lat_deg + 90) / (big edge_lat_deg + 90) * (big size / 2).
